job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Wendy Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good morning. I live in Kestrel Hill with my parents and my grandmother, above our family's fabric shop on Market Street. I get up for prayers, help open the shop, then spend the morning writing job applications at the counter between customers. I finished accounting at Kestrel Hill College last summer, with a pass and no internship. I'm engaged, and we hope to marry next spring, so I'd like a steady job in an office near home. I don't use AI. I like to do things myself and be sure they're right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's sensible. A lot of noise, and the real work carries on. Good accountants are still needed, and good people should be hired, apprenticed and taught properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious about the waiting. There are jobs around, but I've had no offer, and my fiance's family asks politely. I want to contribute to our home, not be the one waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to the local firms, five a week, and visit them in person with my CV, which my father says works better. I'd keep helping in the shop, doing the books for my family. And I'd ask our community elders if anyone knows a firm that takes trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little heavy. I don't complain, but I do notice every week that passes. It's not fear, it's more like a stone in my shoe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the wedding plans and the job hunt together.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our family is a bit anxious for me, in the kind way. My mother says, work will come. My father says, be patient. And my fiance says he's happy to wait, which is a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of job would you say yes to straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local firm with a clear training path, where I can qualify, with colleagues who'd treat me properly. Even if pay is modest at first. A steady place matters more than a flashy one.

fieldNote: Her worry is **time and the wedding**, not AI, and her tone is gentle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be careful. If software does the checking, someone still has to be responsible for what's signed. I'd say firms owe their young staff real training, not just a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. The checking of figures is the exact work that first-year accountants learn on. If a program does it, why would a firm pay me to learn? I've never used these tools, and I'm slow to trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my college tutor to show me one program, just one, and I'd practise on my family's shop accounts. I'd look for firms that still take trainees, and I'd apply to the smaller ones. I'd also ask about a post in a bank branch, where people still talk to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like to be pushed into things. But I also don't want to be the one left behind, so I'm in two minds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your accounting work could a program do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep the shop's books on paper and be right, but I'd be slow. A program could do it in minutes. I don't love that, but I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the tools, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little, if someone I trust shows me, and if I can check the answer myself. I'd never accept a number I couldn't verify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is not for companies alone to decide. Governments, families and communities should be consulted. I'd also say work has dignity, and people shouldn't be left with only handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. Accounting is all thinking work, so it goes first. I've done my degree, and the firms I wanted wouldn't need me. I'd be left with the shop, which is honest work but small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost, and talk with my fiance about delaying the wedding plans, which breaks my heart. I'd put my savings in the safest place. I'd ask my father whether the shop could take on more, and look at hands-on work like office management, which lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray a lot, and I'd cry, then I'd get up and open the shop. That's how my grandmother lived through hard years, and it's how I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say we have the shop, we have each other, and we'll manage. My mother would feed everyone. My grandmother would say her own mother lived through worse. They'd make me feel less alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the wedding change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd want a smaller wedding, not a postponed one, if the money allows. Starting a family on a hopeful note matters to us. But we wouldn't spend on anything showy.

People shouldn't be left with only handouts.

fieldNote: Her fear is real but wrapped in **family resilience** and faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, but only if people use it. Churches, mosques, schools and employers should help people retrain. And parents should speak to their children honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but not hopeless. If I get a job in the next year, I'd have a few years to become more than a number checker, someone who advises families and shops. If I don't, the shop is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any steady accounting post, even a small one. I'd learn one program at a time with help from my tutor. I'd marry next spring, as planned, and keep our home costs low. I'd also help my family's shop get its accounts onto simple software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like having a long road with weather ahead. You can see it, so you wear a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we can plan. We'll marry, we'll save, and we'll keep the shop as a base. He'd say he's with me in this, and that matters more than any job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to your fiance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be scrambling. With five, I'd keep the wedding and learn at my pace.

say: Five years is something, but only if **communities and employers** help people retrain.
Parents should speak honestly to their children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long warning, and we should use it wisely. Young people should be given apprenticeships and trade skills as well as degrees. I'd say a society that cares for its families will manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite settled. By 2036 I'd be 33 with children, a home, and a skill. I'd want my work to be the kind where people still choose to speak to a person, like advising families on money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a trainee post, qualify, and learn the tools slowly. I'd marry and start saving for a home. I'd continue to help at the shop. I'd also take a course in financial advice for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. Ten years is time to live a normal life, with a bit of care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What do you hope for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my children's future. I'd want my children to learn to work with their hands and their minds both. And I'd worry about what money means when machines make everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still be slow with technology, but ten years lets me learn it slowly and safely.

say: It's a long warning and we should use it wisely, with **apprenticeships** and trade skills for the young.
A society that cares for its families will manage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's too fast for families, for the shop, and for me. What would help is time, training places at local firms, communities that help each other, and work that gives people dignity, not just payments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I just think it should serve families and not the other way round. I'd like to be shown by someone I trust.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I just think it should serve families and not the other way round.
portrait: Wendy is a **23-year-old** accounting graduate living above her family's fabric shop in Kestrel Hill and engaged to be married next spring.
She is **traditional**: faith, family and work with dignity matter more to her than handouts.
She is **resistant** to new tools, avoids AI and will try one only if someone she trusts shows her.
She moves from uneasy to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, and lets her family and faith carry her.
With more time she keeps the wedding, learns slowly and aims at advice work for families.
biggestWorry: Her biggest worry is **AGI by 2028**, which is too fast for her family, the shop and her wedding plans.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, training places at local firms, and communities that help each other.
